blocks.title: About this page
blocks.text: Written for this site against the official GATE 2027 CS syllabus from IIT Madras. The questions are original and in the style of GATE: they drill the concepts GATE repeats, they are not copies of past papers. If the official syllabus changes, the official PDF wins.

The **sample space** S is the set of all outcomes, an **event** is a subset of S, and P assigns each event a number with P(S) = 1, P(A) ≥ 0 and additivity for disjoint events. When all outcomes are equally likely, P(A) = |A| / |S|, so most basic problems are counting problems (see the Discrete Mathematics counting section).

| Rule | Formula |
|---|---|
| Complement | P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A) |
| Addition | P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) |
| Mutually exclusive | P(A ∩ B) = 0, so P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) |
| Independent | P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B) |
| Neither occurs | 1 − P(A ∪ B) |
| Three events | P(A∪B∪C) = ΣP − ΣP(pairs) + P(A∩B∩C) |

Two events with non-zero probability can **never** be both. If A and B are mutually exclusive and P(A), P(B) > 0, then P(A ∩ B) = 0 ≠ P(A)P(B), so they are dependent: knowing A happened tells you B did not.
blocks.title: Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive

blocks.text:
### Standard experiments

- **Two dice:** 36 outcomes. Sum 7 has 6 ways (the most likely), sum 2 or 12 has 1. Sum s has 6 − |s − 7| ways.
- **Cards:** 52 cards, 4 suits of 13, 4 kings, 12 face cards, 26 red.
- **Coins:** n tosses give 2ⁿ outcomes, and exactly k heads occur in C(n, k) of them.
- **Without replacement:** multiply conditional probabilities, or count with combinations. P(both aces) = (4/52)(3/51) = 1/221 = C(4,2)/C(52,2).

- **"At least one" → 1 − P(none).** Almost always faster.
- **Adjacent arrangements:** glue the pair into one block, multiply by the internal orderings. For 1 and 2 adjacent in a permutation of n: 2·(n − 1)! / n! = 2/n.
- **Linearity of expectation needs no independence.** To count a total, add up indicator variables. The expected number of fixed points of a random permutation is n · (1/n) = 1 for every n.
- **Symmetry shortcuts:** the probability the maximum of n distinct random numbers is at position k is 1/n; each of two people is equally likely to be "ahead".
- **Distinct values:** n draws with replacement from m values are all different with probability m(m−1)…(m−n+1) / mⁿ.
blocks.title: Probability cheat codes

blocks.text:
P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), defined when P(B) > 0. Rearranged, this is the **multiplication rule** P(A ∩ B) = P(B) P(A | B). Events A and B are independent exactly when P(A | B) = P(A).

**Total probability.** If B₁, …, Bₙ partition the sample space, then P(A) = Σ P(Bᵢ) P(A | Bᵢ).

**Bayes' theorem.** P(Bᵢ | A) = P(Bᵢ) P(A | Bᵢ) / Σⱼ P(Bⱼ) P(A | Bⱼ).

blocks.title: Tree for Bayes questions

blocks.text:
For the tree above, P(defective) = 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.032, and P(machine A | defective) = 0.012 / 0.032 = 3/8. Multiply along a branch, add across branches, then divide.

### Classic puzzles

| Puzzle | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Two children, at least one is a boy, both boys | 1/3 | outcomes BB, BG, GB equally likely |
| Two children, the **elder** is a boy, both boys | 1/2 | only the other child is uncertain |
| Monty Hall, always switch | 2/3 | your first pick is right with 1/3 and the host's choice carries the rest |
| Rare disease, accurate test | low | a small prevalence swamps a small false-positive rate |

- **Draw the tree.** Write the prior on the first branches and the likelihood on the second, then multiply along the paths that match the evidence.
- **Use natural frequencies:** imagine 10 000 people. With a prevalence of 1%, 100 are ill; 99 of those test positive. Of the 9 900 healthy, 5% (495) test positive. P(ill | positive) = 99 / (99 + 495) = 1/6.
- **Posterior ≤ 1/2 when the prior is tiny** unless the false-positive rate is much smaller than the prior.
- **Without replacement,** the second draw depends on the first, so use P(2nd | 1st), not P(2nd).
- **Independence check:** P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B). If given P(A | B) = P(A), you are done.
blocks.title: Bayes cheat codes

blocks.text:
A **random variable** X maps outcomes to numbers. A discrete X has a pmf p(x) = P(X = x), and a continuous X has a pdf f(x) with P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = ∫ f. The cdf is F(x) = P(X ≤ x).

| Quantity | Discrete | Continuous |
|---|---|---|
| Mean E[X] | Σ x p(x) | ∫ x f(x) dx |
| E[g(X)] | Σ g(x) p(x) | ∫ g(x) f(x) dx |
| Variance | E[X²] − (E[X])² | the same |
| Standard deviation | √Var(X) | |

### Rules

- **E[aX + b] = a E[X] + b**, and **Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X)**. Adding a constant changes the mean but not the spread.
- **E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] always**, even for dependent variables.
- **Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 Cov(X, Y).** For independent X, Y, Var(aX + bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y): the coefficient is **squared** and the variances **always add**, even for X − Y.
- **E[XY] = E[X] E[Y] if X and Y are independent.** The converse is false: uncorrelated does not imply independent.
- **For a non-negative integer X:** E[X] = Σₖ₌₁ P(X ≥ k).
- Normalisation: Σ p(x) = 1 or ∫ f = 1. Use this to find an unknown constant first.

- **Variance of a sum of independent variables:** the sign inside does not matter. Var(2X − Y) = 4 Var(X) + Var(Y).
- **E[(X − c)²] = Var(X) + (E[X] − c)².** This is the shortcut for any "mean squared deviation about a point".
- **Expected maximum of two fair dice** = Σ k (2k − 1) / 36 = 161/36. Build the pmf from "max ≤ k has probability (k/6)²".
- **Fair die:** mean 7/2, variance 35/12.
- **Indicator trick:** X = Σ Iᵢ, so E[X] = Σ P(Iᵢ = 1). Perfect for "expected number of …" questions.
blocks.title: Random variable cheat codes

blocks.text:
| Distribution | Models | pmf or pdf | Mean | Variance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bernoulli(p) | one yes/no trial | p, 1 − p | p | p(1 − p) |
| Binomial(n, p) | successes in n independent trials | C(n, k) pᵏ (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ | np | np(1 − p) |
| Geometric(p) | trials up to the first success | (1 − p)ᵏ⁻¹ p | 1/p | (1 − p)/p² |
| Poisson(λ) | events in a fixed interval | e⁻λ λᵏ / k! | λ | λ |
| Uniform(a, b) | equally likely over an interval | 1/(b − a) | (a + b)/2 | (b − a)²/12 |
| Exponential(λ) | waiting time between events | λ e⁻λx for x ≥ 0 | 1/λ | 1/λ² |
| Normal(μ, σ²) | sums and measurements | bell curve | μ | σ² |

### Key properties

- **Binomial and Poisson:** Poisson(np) approximates Binomial(n, p) when n is large and p is small. Sums of independent Poissons add their λ.
- **Geometric and exponential are memoryless:** P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). The expected additional wait does not depend on how long you have already waited.
- **Exponential tail:** P(X > x) = e⁻λx. The median is ln 2 / λ.
- **Poisson process:** events at rate r per unit time. The number in time t is Poisson(rt), and the gap between events is Exponential(r).
- **Normal:** symmetric, so mean = median = mode. About **68%** of the mass lies within one σ, **95%** within two, **99.7%** within three. Standardise with Z = (X − μ) / σ. P(Z < 1) = 0.8413 and P(Z < 1.96) = 0.975. If X ~ N(μ, σ²) then aX + b ~ N(aμ + b, a²σ²), and independent normals add means and variances.

- **Match the question to the table in 5 seconds:** fixed number of trials → binomial; "first success" → geometric; "events per unit time" → Poisson; "time between events" → exponential.
- **Given mean and variance of a binomial,** divide: Var/mean = 1 − p. A mean of 12 and a variance of 8 give p = 1/3 and n = 36.
- **Poisson with λ = 2:** P(0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.135, P(1) = 2e⁻² ≈ 0.271.
- **Exponential with mean μ:** P(X > μ) = e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368 for any μ.
- **Uniform conditional:** inside an interval, probabilities are proportional to lengths. P(X > 7 | X > 3) on [0, 10] is 3/7.
- **Geometric trap:** this table counts trials, including the success. If a question counts failures, the mean is (1 − p)/p instead.
blocks.title: Distribution cheat codes

sections.title: Descriptive statistics: mean, median, mode, standard deviation

blocks.text:
| Measure | Definition | Effect of y = ax + b |
|---|---|---|
| Mean | Σxᵢ / n | ȳ = a x̄ + b |
| Median | middle value of sorted data (average of the two middle values if n is even) | median becomes a·median + b |
| Mode | most frequent value | same transformation |
| Variance | Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² / n (population) | multiplied by a² |
| Standard deviation | √variance | multiplied by \|a\| |

- **Sample variance** divides by n − 1, population variance divides by n. Read the question for which one it means.
- **Empirical relation** for moderately skewed data: Mode ≈ 3 · Median − 2 · Mean.
- **Combined mean** of groups with sizes nᵢ and means mᵢ is Σ nᵢ mᵢ / Σ nᵢ. A mean cannot be combined by averaging averages unless the sizes are equal.
- **First n natural numbers:** mean (n + 1)/2, variance (n² − 1)/12.
- **Removing or adding a value:** recompute from the total. New mean = (old total ∓ value) / new count.
- **Skew:** mean > median > mode for a long right tail, and mean < median < mode for a long left tail.

- **Shift and scale:** the mean follows y = ax + b; the SD follows only |a|. The variance follows a².
- **Variance shortcut:** compute E[X²] − (E[X])². For data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: mean 5, E[X²] = 29, variance = 29 − 25 = 4, SD = 2.
- **Median of even count** = average of the two middle values after sorting. Always sort first.
- **Outliers move the mean, not the median.** If a question asks which statistic is unchanged when the largest value grows, the answer is the median (or the mode).
- **Weighted average > unweighted** when the heavier group has the higher mean.

sections.title: Cheat sheet: Probability and Statistics on one page

blocks.text:
| Topic | Formula or fact |
|---|---|
| Union | P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B) |
| Conditional | P(A ∩ B) / P(B) |
| Bayes | P(Bᵢ) P(A \| Bᵢ) / Σ P(Bⱼ) P(A \| Bⱼ) |
| Linear transform | E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b, Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X) |
| Independent sum | Var(aX ± bY) = a² Var(X) + b² Var(Y) |
| Fair die | mean 3.5, variance 35/12 |
| Binomial | np, np(1 − p) |
| Geometric | mean 1/p, variance (1 − p)/p² |
| Poisson | mean = variance = λ |
| Uniform(a, b) | (a + b)/2, (b − a)²/12 |
| Exponential(λ) | mean 1/λ, P(X > x) = e⁻λx, memoryless |
| Normal | 68 – 95 – 99.7, Z = (X − μ)/σ |
| Mode estimate | 3 · median − 2 · mean |
| Natural numbers 1…n | mean (n + 1)/2, variance (n² − 1)/12 |

60 original GATE-style questions on 7 areas. Pick an answer to see why it is right and which trap catches people. The marks shown are what a question like this would carry in GATE; in the real exam a wrong 1-mark MCQ costs 1/3 mark and a wrong 2-mark MCQ costs 2/3.

items.q: *(1 mark)* Two fair six-sided dice are thrown. The probability that the sum of the two numbers is 8 is
items.w: The pairs (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) give 5 favourable outcomes out of 36.

items.q: *(1 mark)* One card is drawn from a standard deck of 52 cards. The probability that it is a king or a heart is
items.w: 4 kings + 13 hearts − 1 (the king of hearts is counted twice) = 16 favourable cards, and 16/52 = 4/13.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A 3-digit number is chosen uniformly at random from 100 to 999. The probability that all three digits are different is
items.w: Distinct-digit numbers: 9 choices for the hundreds digit, 9 for the tens (0 is allowed but not the first digit), 8 for the units, so 648. There are 900 numbers in total, and 648/900 = 0.72.

items.q: *(1 mark)* A fair coin is tossed three times. The probability of getting at least one head is
items.w: Use the complement: P(no head) = (1/2)³ = 1/8, so the answer is 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Three people are each born on a uniformly random day of the week, independently. The probability that all three were born on different days is
items.w: The first person can be born on any day. The second must avoid 1 day (6/7) and the third must avoid 2 days (5/7). So 6/7 × 5/7 = 30/49.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard 52-card deck. The probability that both are aces is
*(2 marks)* A random permutation of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} is written in a row. The probability that 1 and 2 are next to each other is
items.w: Glue 1 and 2 into a block with 2 internal orders: 2 × 4! = 48 favourable permutations out of 5! = 120, which is 2/5.

items.q: *(2 marks)* For events A and B, P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. The probability that neither A nor B occurs is
*(1 mark)* Events A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.4. Then P(A ∪ B) equals
items.w: For mutually exclusive events P(A ∩ B) = 0, so the probabilities simply add: 0.3 + 0.4 = 0.7. (0.12 would be P(A)P(B), which applies to independent events.)

items.q: *(2 marks)* The numbers 1 to n (n ≥ 2) are put into a random order. The expected number of positions i whose entry equals i (fixed points) is
items.w: Let Iᵢ be the indicator that position i holds i, so P(Iᵢ = 1) = 1/n. By linearity of expectation E = n × (1/n) = 1, whatever n is, and even though the indicators are dependent.

items.q: *(1 mark)* P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.3. Then P(A | B) is
items.w: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) = 0.3 / 0.5 = 0.6. This equals P(A), so A and B are independent.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A family has two children, and at least one of them is a boy. Assuming boys and girls are equally likely, the probability that both are boys is
items.w: The equally likely outcomes (elder, younger) are BB, BG, GB, GG. "At least one boy" removes GG, leaving 3 outcomes of which 1 is BB.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Machine A makes 60% of the items and 2% of its items are defective. Machine B makes the other 40% and 5% of its items are defective. An item is picked at random and found defective. The probability it came from machine A is

*(2 marks)* 1% of a population has a disease. A test gives a positive result for 99% of ill people and for 5% of healthy people. A person tests positive. The probability that the person has the disease is
items.w: P(positive) = 0.01 × 0.99 + 0.99 × 0.05 = 0.0594. P(disease | positive) = 0.0099 / 0.0594 = 1/6. Most positives come from the large healthy group.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Urn 1 holds 3 red and 2 blue balls. Urn 2 holds 1 red and 4 blue balls. An urn is chosen at random and one ball is drawn. The probability that the ball is red is
*(2 marks)* In the previous setting (urn 1: 3 red, 2 blue; urn 2: 1 red, 4 blue; urn chosen at random), the ball drawn is red. The probability that it came from urn 1 is
*(2 marks)* Two cards are drawn one after the other without replacement from a standard deck. Given that the first card is an ace, the probability that the second card is also an ace is
items.w: After one ace is removed, 3 aces remain among 51 cards: 3/51 = 1/17.

items.q: *(2 marks)* In the Monty Hall game, a prize is behind one of three doors and you choose one. The host, who knows where the prize is, opens another door that has no prize and offers a switch. The probability of winning if you always switch is
items.w: Your first choice is right with probability 1/3. Whenever it is wrong (2/3), the host's reveal leaves the prize on the only other closed door, so switching wins.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5. P(A ∪ B) is
*(2 marks)* P(A) = 1/3, P(B | A) = 1/2 and P(B | Aᶜ) = 1/4. Then P(B) equals
*(1 mark)* The expected value of the number shown by one throw of a fair six-sided die is
*(2 marks)* The variance of the number shown by one throw of a fair six-sided die is
*(2 marks)* A random variable X has E[X] = 3 and Var(X) = 4. Then E[(X − 1)²] equals
items.w: E[(X − c)²] = Var(X) + (E[X] − c)² = 4 + (3 − 1)² = 8. Equivalently E[X²] = 13, so E[X²] − 2E[X] + 1 = 13 − 6 + 1 = 8.

items.q: *(1 mark)* If Var(X) = 2, then Var(3X + 7) is
items.w: Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X) = 9 × 2 = 18. The constant 7 does not change the spread.

items.q: *(2 marks)* X and Y are independent with Var(X) = 3 and Var(Y) = 5. Then Var(2X − Y) is
items.w: For independent variables Var(2X − Y) = 4 Var(X) + Var(Y) = 12 + 5 = 17. The minus sign does not turn the variance of Y into a subtraction.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A discrete random variable takes the values k = 1, 2, 3, 4 with P(X = k) = c·k. Its expected value is
items.w: The probabilities sum to 1, so c(1 + 2 + 3 + 4) = 1 and c = 1/10. E[X] = Σ k · k/10 = (1 + 4 + 9 + 16)/10 = 3.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A continuous random variable has density f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and 0 elsewhere. Its mean is
items.w: E[X] = ∫₀¹ x · 2x dx = 2 ∫₀¹ x² dx = 2 · 1/3 = 2/3.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Two fair six-sided dice are thrown. The expected value of the larger of the two numbers is
*(2 marks)* Which of the following statements is TRUE for random variables X and Y?
o: If X and Y are independent, then Cov(X, Y) = 0
E[XY] = E[X] E[Y] implies that X and Y are independent
If Cov(X, Y) = 0, then X and Y are independent
Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) for every X and Y
items.w: Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance (or E[XY] = E[X]E[Y]) does not imply independence. Variances add only when the covariance is zero.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A random variable X takes values in {0, 1, 2, 3} with P(X > 0) = 0.8, P(X > 1) = 0.5 and P(X > 2) = 0.2. Then E[X] is
items.w: For non-negative integer values, E[X] = P(X ≥ 1) + P(X ≥ 2) + P(X ≥ 3) = 0.8 + 0.5 + 0.2 = 1.5.

items.q: *(1 mark)* X ~ Binomial(10, 0.5). Then P(X = 5) equals
*(2 marks)* A fair coin is tossed 5 times. The probability of getting at least 2 heads is
*(1 mark)* X ~ Binomial(20, 0.3). The variance of X is
items.w: Variance = np(1 − p) = 20 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 4.2. (6 is the mean.)

items.q: *(2 marks)* A fair die is thrown repeatedly until a six appears. The expected number of throws is
items.w: The number of trials to the first success has a geometric distribution with mean 1/p = 6.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A fair die is rolled repeatedly. The probability that the first six appears on exactly the third roll is
items.w: Two non-sixes then a six: (5/6)(5/6)(1/6) = 25/216.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Four independent trials each succeed with probability 1/3. The probability of exactly 2 successes is
*(2 marks)* A binomial random variable has mean 12 and variance 8. The number of trials n is
*(2 marks)* Independent trials succeed with probability 0.25 each, and the first 5 trials all failed. The expected number of additional trials until the first success is
items.w: The geometric distribution is memoryless, so the past failures are irrelevant. The expected wait is still 1/p = 4.

items.q: *(1 mark)* X is Poisson with mean 2. P(X = 0) is approximately
items.w: P(X = 0) = e⁻² ≈ 0.1353. (e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368 would be the answer for mean 1.)

items.q: *(2 marks)* A Poisson random variable has mean 3. Its variance is
items.w: A Poisson distribution has its mean equal to its variance, both equal to λ.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The number of requests per second to a server is Poisson with mean 4. The probability of at least one request in a given second is approximately
*(2 marks)* The lifetime of a component is exponentially distributed with mean 10 hours. The probability that it lasts longer than 10 hours is approximately
*(2 marks)* The waiting time at a counter is exponential with a mean of 5 minutes. A customer has already waited 3 minutes. The expected additional waiting time is
items.w: The exponential distribution is memoryless: the remaining wait has the same distribution as a new wait, with mean 5 minutes.

items.q: *(1 mark)* X is uniformly distributed on the interval [2, 8]. The variance of X is
items.w: Var = (b − a)²/12 = 36/12 = 3. (The mean is 5.)

items.q: *(2 marks)* X is uniform on [0, 10]. P(X > 7 | X > 3) equals
items.w: Given X > 3, X is uniform on [3, 10], of length 7. The part above 7 has length 3, so the probability is 3/7.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Calls arrive as a Poisson process at a rate of 2 per minute. The probability that no call arrives in a 1.5-minute interval is approximately
items.w: The number of calls in 1.5 minutes is Poisson with mean 3, so P(0) = e⁻³ ≈ 0.0498.

items.q: *(2 marks)* X is exponentially distributed with rate λ. The median of X is
items.w: The median m satisfies 1 − e^(−λm) = 1/2, so e^(−λm) = 1/2 and m = ln 2 / λ ≈ 0.69/λ, less than the mean 1/λ.

items.q: *(1 mark)* For a normal distribution, approximately what fraction of the values lie within two standard deviations of the mean?
items.w: The empirical rule: about 68% within one σ, 95% within two σ and 99.7% within three σ.

items.q: *(2 marks)* X ~ N(50, 100), i.e. mean 50 and variance 100. Using P(Z < 1) = 0.8413, P(X > 60) is approximately
*(2 marks)* X ~ N(4, 9), meaning mean 4 and variance 9. The random variable Y = 2X − 1 is distributed as
items.w: The mean is 2 × 4 − 1 = 7 and the variance is 2² × 9 = 36. A linear function of a normal variable is normal.

items.q: *(2 marks)* X ~ N(1, 4) and Y ~ N(2, 5) are independent (second parameter = variance). Then X + Y is distributed as
items.w: For independent normals the means add (1 + 2 = 3) and so do the variances (4 + 5 = 9).

items.q: *(1 mark)* Z is a standard normal variable. P(Z ≤ −1.5) is equal to
items.w: The standard normal density is symmetric about 0, so the left tail below −1.5 has the same area as the right tail above 1.5.

items.q: *(2 marks)* Which of the following is TRUE for every normal distribution?
o: Its mean, median and mode coincide
Its mean is greater than its median
items.w: The normal density is symmetric and unimodal about μ, so mean = median = mode and the skewness is 0. Variance equal to mean is a property of the Poisson distribution.

items.q: *(1 mark)* The median of the data 12, 5, 9, 20, 7, 15 is
items.w: Sorted: 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 20. There are six values, so the median is the average of the middle two: (9 + 12)/2 = 10.5. (11.33 is the mean.)

items.q: *(2 marks)* The mean of 5 numbers is 20. When one of them, 30, is removed, the mean of the remaining numbers becomes
items.w: The total was 100. Removing 30 leaves 70 over 4 numbers: 70/4 = 17.5.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The population standard deviation of the data 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 is
items.w: The mean is 5. The squared deviations are 9, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 4, 16, which sum to 32. The variance is 32/8 = 4 and the standard deviation is 2.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The values x have mean 10 and standard deviation 2. The values y = 3x + 4 then have mean and standard deviation
items.w: The mean follows the full transformation: 3 × 10 + 4 = 34. The standard deviation is multiplied by |3| and unaffected by the shift: 6.

items.q: *(2 marks)* A moderately skewed data set has mean 33 and median 30. Using the empirical relation, its mode is approximately
items.w: Mode ≈ 3 × Median − 2 × Mean = 90 − 66 = 24.

items.q: *(2 marks)* The variance of the first 10 natural numbers 1, 2, …, 10 (treated as a whole population) is
items.w: The variance of 1…n is (n² − 1)/12 = 99/12 = 8.25. (9.17 would be the sample variance, which divides by n − 1.)

items.q: *(2 marks)* A class has two groups. Group A has 20 students with mean marks 60 and group B has 30 students with mean marks 70. The mean marks of the whole class is
items.w: Combined mean = (20 × 60 + 30 × 70) / 50 = (1200 + 2100) / 50 = 66. The larger group pulls the mean above 65.

blocks.text: #### Cheat sheet: Probability and Statistics on one page

items.question: A test detects a disease 99% of the time and gives a false positive 5% of the time. The disease affects 1% of people. What is P(disease | positive)?
items.answer: (0.01 × 0.99) / (0.01 × 0.99 + 0.99 × 0.05) = 99 / 594 = 1/6, about 17%. The healthy majority produces far more false positives than the few ill people produce true positives.

items.question: Why is Var(X − Y) equal to Var(X) + Var(Y) for independent X and Y?
items.answer: Var(−Y) = (−1)² Var(Y) = Var(Y), and covariance is zero, so the variances add. Spreads accumulate whether you add or subtract.

items.question: A fair die is rolled until a six appears. What are the mean and variance of the number of rolls?
items.answer: Geometric with p = 1/6: mean = 1/p = 6 and variance = (1 − p)/p² = (5/6) / (1/36) = 30.

items.question: What does "memoryless" mean for an exponential random variable?
items.answer: P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t). If a bus has not come in the last s minutes, the remaining wait has the same distribution as when you started. No other continuous distribution has this property.
